messages.subject_clean: Error in inla model fitting - model with random effect and temporal correlation
messages.body_plain:
Hi group,

I am trying to model a distance between pairs of animals, dxyz, and for each pair of animals I have distances measured every two seconds, since the moment animals started echo locating looking for food. The distance between the animals increases up to a point as a smooth function of time and then decreases until they are back together. There's also a fixed factor type. It seems to me animal pair needs to be included as a random effect, and there will be temporal correlation within each pair. I tried the model below

#define each formula component
#response
y="dxyz"
#fixed factor
fixed="type"
#smooth effect of time
st="f(tsv,model='rw1')"
#the correlation over time inside pair
inladat$tsv2=inladat$tsv
cotip="f(pid,model='iid',group=tsv2,control.group = list(model = 'ar1'))"
#full formula
ff=as.formula(paste0(y,"~",fixed,"+",st,"+",cotip))
#run model
inlaMOD1=inla(formula=ff,data=inladat)

but I end up with an error

`Error in inla(fSor, data = inladat, control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE)) :
  Error in the values of `group'; not in [1,...,2190]"`

I suspect this error arises because not all pairs have the same number of observations, but I am not 100% sure that is the case. So my questions are:

1. Does the model look reasonable for the problem described?
2. Is the problem related to pairs of animals having different numbers of observations? I can't understand why that would be a problem in general, since it seems reasonable to me to have a longitudinal study for which the number of observations per subject is not the same, but for which the temporal correlation within units across times would be the same across units.

I am a inla novice, so any help regarding this matter would be greatly appreciated. Many thanks in advance.

Best,

Tiago

> How can i compute total CPO for the model for comparing two models?

Hi,

yes, its of length 2*n, since this is the length of the linear
predictor.

total cpo. you can add them, this would be the normal approach.
if y[i]=NA, then cpo[i]=NA, so you should ignore them.

>
> Do you know if the criterias like DIC,WAIC, marginal likelihood and
> etc are logical for comparing my two models: joint model with two
> likelihhood and other one with ignoring missing value?

I would not worry about missing values in the response, as DIC and WAIC
are computed for the observed ones only. it should not make a different
either, if you have two different likelihoods.

hope this helps,

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] ar1 vs rw1
messages.body_plain:
If the data are well represented by a random walk, then yes, those two models should be very similar to that, with a large ar-coefficient.

Setting a sumtozero constrain for _all_ ar1 models is tempting, but is the wrong thing to do in many situations.
With only a single realisation, it comes down to prior information and domain specific knowledge; if the model is only used for interpolation/smoothing, then it doesn’t matter as much if the interpretation of each model component is different, but since imposing constraints fundamentally _changes_ the model (and this is also true of the rw1 model itself; there was a discussion about this a few months back, regarding intrinsic random field models, that I believe was on this list...) it’s not a universally appropriate approach.

The only “objective” way out is to have multiple realisations, where e.g. the intercept parameter is the same for each realisation, so that the model is properly identifiable.

Finn

Hi,
The standard deviation of a transformation is _not_ the transformation of the standard deviation, so exp(sd) in your code is incorrect.
Quantiles transform like that, but not moments.
If your posteriors are skewed, use quantiles instead of moments when possible.
The moments of fitted.values are the moments of the transformed distribution, so those are the ones you should use if you need them.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

For practical convenience, I almost always use quantiles (including median instead of mean). Because I do not know what is the "right parametrisation", x, or exp(x), sigma or variance. With quantiles, you can transform them back and forth at will.

You can usually report "median" ("0.025 quantile", "0.975 quantile") when you do applications, e.g: 7 (5.4, 20)

For spatial plots you then need 2 quantile-plots instead of 1 sd-plot, so here it is more debatable what to do. But the sd plot on fitted.value-scale may not represent what you think it represents! The "uncertainty" on this scale is often not "symmetric", making sd a less useful summary statistic (quantiles are still good).

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka

messages.subject_clean: Accounting for spatial measurement errors in INLA
messages.body_plain:
Dear All -

I've got a question about INLA's capacity to deal with potential errors in geolocations (e.g., latitude and longitude).

Zhang et al. (2016) highlight the fact that there may be spatial measurement errors in geolocations for point process or geostatistical data which can include instrumental errors, geocoding errors and aggregated outcomes at a specific location (https://ij-healthgeographics.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12942-016-0049-5). Basically, I was wondering if there is any way INLA can account for geolocations that are measured with some error?  Somewhat like an “errors in variables” for the locations rather than for the covariates.  If so, at what stage would this error be specified (e.g., mesh creation)?

Many thanks for any assistance,

Paul

Here are my 2 cents.

I tend to display 4 maps.
1) the mean or median to display the estimates itself.
2) the 2.5% percentile. High values on this map indicate areas where you are pretty sure that the phenomenon is present.
3) the 97.5 percentile. Low values on this map indicate areas where you are pretty sure that the phenomenon is absent.
4) the difference (identity link) or ratio (log link) between the 97.5% percentile and 2.5% percentile. This displays the uncertainty.

messages.subject: Appropriate pc.prec priors for binomial model with several sources of covariance
messages.subject_clean: Appropriate pc.prec priors for binomial model with several sources of covariance
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone on the r-inla team (and other interested parties),

I've been exploring using r-inla for a number of models in my work (as an ecologist), and I am really loving it. I have been working things out through reading tutorials and this forum, but I am now ready to start posting question about things I can't quite figure out. Expect a fair number of questions from me in the coming months. My first one is fairly general:

I am modeling a binary response (binomial with trials = 1) with a number of different sources of covariance, as well as several fixed effects. The covariance structures are spatial (for which I am using a spde2.pcmatern), phylogenetic (using generic0 with an inverse phylogenetic covariance matrix), and iid (for my individual species). I am struggling to choose a good prior for the phylogenetic and iid component. I want to use a PC prior, as is recommended by the authors of this package, but was wondering what guidelines exist for choosing good values of alpha and mu? The way we usually use random effects models in my field is to 'control for' non-independence created by phylogeny. In other words, we are concerned that some of our fixed effect variables and our response have shared phylogenetic structure, which could lead us to believe we have more independent observations that we think we do. In this situation, what priors would you recommend? My concern is that a pc prior that too strongly penalizes the random effects will shrink them away, leaving only the fixed effects, even if the fixed effects are confounded with the phylogenetic effect (which is what we are trying to 'account for'). But perhaps this is a false concern? Maximum likelihood methods are more commonly used in my field and my understanding is using a uniform prior should give me something closer to the ML model, and I can do this by using a large lambda value on the PC prior (eg. param = c(1, 0.99))? I have tried this, and compared to param = c(1, 0.01), and the two models have fairly different results for the random effects (but the fixed effects are similar, which is good). But maybe something in between those two more extreme priors would be better? What would be a good choice to make the phylogenetic effect more comparable to the spatial (under the pc.matern model)? Is there any guidelines for this, or should I be trying a variety of priors and then choosing based on some criteria of the model fit? Any guidance on this issue would be greatly appreciated (even just pointing to a tutorial or article I may have missed). Note: I am using constr = TRUE on all the f()'s.

Thanks very much for all your time and effort put into this package! Cheers,

Russell

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Appropriate pc.prec priors for binomial model with several sources of covariance
messages.body_plain:
My general thoughts on this:

If you want to fit one good model, according to you prior knowledge and modeling preferences, you select one prior (for each component) and fit one model.

However, you want to study the fixed effects (or some specific model component) and draw conclusions based on the results of this component. What you want (what I would want in your place) is robustness/stability. To study how the fixed effects are impacted by the random effect, I think running several models with several different priors is a good thing! Note that, if you have sufficiently complex random effects, all other parts of the model will disappear (become insignificant), and if you have too restrictive random effects/likelihood, all your fixed effects may become significant.

What I want is results that are stable with respect to a "set of reasonable priors". Instead of one good model with a "very small p value" I want to see that my 95% intervals exclude zero, no matter what other (reasonable) alternative explanations (random effects/priors) I include in the model.

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka

Hello,
Could someone please help me interpret the mgamma prior for the negative binomial size parameter.
The way I interpret it is that the density is over /theta which can be converted to the negative binomial size parameter as exp(-log(theta)) see R code below for a plot.
It is also not clear to me what the interpretation for the lambda parameter is, though I gather that smaller values of lambda put greater density near zero, whereas greater values will shrink the negative binomial towards a poisson distribution.
Thanks,
Chris

R code to plot priors:

n <- 1000
theta <- seq(0,5, length.out = n)
d1 <- inla.pc.dgamma(theta, lambda = 7) #default?
d2 <- inla.pc.dgamma(theta, lambda = 0.1) #more weight on overdispersion
d3 <- inla.pc.dgamma(theta, lambda = 70) #less weight on overdispersion

plot(exp(-log(theta)),d1, xlab= "negbin size", ylab = "density", type = 'l')
lines(exp(-log(theta)),d2, col = "red")
lines(exp(-log(theta)),d3, col = "green")

messages.subject_clean: Fitting an ARIMA process in INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hello!

I'm trying to see how feasible it would be to fit a full ARIMA process in INLA. In the econometrics literature, they define an MA process as lags of the errors, and so I thought if I could use INLA's AR(1) model to analogously fit that.

Here's a snippet of code where I simulated an AR(1) and an ARIMA(1,0,1):

  require(INLA)
  require(data.table)

  ## AR and MA params
  rho = 0.8
  phi = 0.3
  prec = 10
  n = 1000

  ## Simulate ARIMA(1,0,1)
  dt1 = as.vector(arima.sim(list(order = c(1,0,1), ar = rho, ma = phi), n = n,
                 sd = sqrt(1/prec)))

  ## Simulate ARIMA(1,0,0)
  dt2 = as.vector(arima.sim(list(order = c(1,0,0), ar = rho), n = n,
                  sd = sqrt(1/prec)))

  ## Make sure we can recover params by fitting the ARIMAs
  arima(dt1, c(1,0,1))
  arima(dt2, c(1,0,0))

Here's the results from first fitting an AR(1) process with the second dataset. I fit the AR(1) using both the 'ar1' model and also by using the lag of the variable.
  ## Fit the AR(1) from dt2 in INLA
  ar1_dt2 <- data.table(y = dt2, t = 1:n)
  ar1_dt2[, lag_y := shift(y)]

  ## Fit with model
    inla_ar1_dt2_1 <- inla(formula = y ~ f(t, model = 'ar1'),
                         data = ar1_dt2)

    summary(inla_ar1_dt2_1)

  ## Fit as lag FE
    inla_ar1_dt2_2 <- inla(formula = y ~ lag_y,
                           data = ar1_dt2)

    summary(inla_ar1_dt2_2)

### Both the models recovered the AR(1) parameter in either the FE or the RE ###

The results are quite similar and this is where I got a bit confused, because an AR(1) on residuals versus an AR(1) on the dependent variable aren't equivalent right (or maybe I'm wrong..)?

Finally, I attempt to fit an ARIMA(1,0,1) by including the lag value and the 'ar1' model (with the hope that the former will pick up the AR(1) part, and the latter will pick up the MA(1) part):
  ## What if we try to fit the ARIMA in INLA?
  arima_dt1  = data.table(y = dt1, t = 1:n)
  arima_dt1[, lag_y := shift(y)]
  inla_arima_dt1 <- inla(formula = y ~ lag_y + f(t, model = 'ar1'),
                       data = arima_dt1)
  summary(inla_arima_dt1)

messages.subject: correct Bayesian updating
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Bayesian updating is a great feature of Bayesian models, and when using INLA, I'd like to do it correctly.

In the example below, am I using the posteriors from model m1 correctly as priors for m2?  I want m2 to be the best model given the data that was used for m1 and m2.  (Of course, the old data might be long gone in a non-trivial example.)

library(INLA)
set.seed(1)
inla.seed = 2

# first data set is used with default priors to fit model m1
x <- 1:100
y <- 5 + 4 * x + rnorm(n=length(x), sd=3)
m1 <- inla(y ~ x, data=data.frame(x, y), control.compute=list(config=TRUE))

# set up priors for m2 fixed-effects parameters based on m1 posteriors
posterior.mean <- function(m, name) m$summary.fixed[name, "mean"]
posterior.prec <- function(m, name) 1/m$summary.fixed[name, "sd"]^2
fixed.priors <- list()
fixed.priors$mean = list()
fixed.priors$prec = list()
for (name in c("(Intercept)", "x")) {
    fixed.priors$mean[[name]] <- posterior.mean(m1, name)
    fixed.priors$prec[[name]] <- posterior.prec(m1, name)
}

# use points from posterior of precision as prior for m2
ih <- m1$internal.marginals.hyperpar[[1]]
table.string <- paste(c("table:", ih[,"x"], ih[,"y"]), collapse=" ")

# new data
x <- seq(from=1, to=100, by=0.5)
y <- 5 + 4 * x + rnorm(n=length(x), sd=3)

# update model with new data
m2 <- inla(y ~ x,
    data=data.frame(x, y),
    control.fixed=fixed.priors,
    control.family=list(hyper=list(prec=list(prior=table.string))))

Thanks!

--
  Ed

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

My thoughts on Bayesian updating:

This is great in theory, but works poorly in practice. Any numerical algorithm chooses a fidelity of approximation of the posterior. Clever algorithms (MCMC/INLA/...) only has a good fidelity where the posterior has large values (to save computational time).

When you fit a second dataset, the posterior contribution from this may be somewhere else than the posterior for the first dataset. This means that the fidelity of the relevant part of the first posterior is extremely poor. And so, we cannot represent (with reasonable high fidelity) the prior for the second dataset.

However, if the second dataset is "very consistent" with the first dataset, only concentrating the distributions more, I think it can work. But you do not know this in advance. Additionally, if everything is Gaussian, it might work.

The easiest way to compute Bayesian updating, I think, is to re-fit the entire dataset1 & dataset2 in a new joint model.

In your code example, I do not think you have taken the posterior correlations into account. E.g. the likelihood (family) parameter is correlated with the fixed effect for "x".

PS: I appreciate being corrected on this, as I have never tried Bayesian updating

Kind regards,
Haakon

messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

I have been playing with a model that models a distance between animals as a function of time (tsv). A tentative model is listed below, and includes a fixed factor (type) and a random effect for animal pair (pid).

inlamod1=inla(formula=dxyz~type+f(pid,model="iid")+f(tsv,model="rw1"),data=inladat)

This is what the smooth term plot looks like - and it seemed to be overfitting to me (as compared to say what a vanilla GAM would)

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-e5bE6zHO40M/Wrjk3ebE1EI/AAAAAAAAYFc/xmqI2pdqf6s0lQL5keGN0S9OHCdDpxgPACLcBGAs/s1600/tsv1.JPG>

I read in https://www.r-bloggers.com/smoothing-a-time-series-with-a-bayesian-model/  how one might go about tweaking the degree of smoothness of the rw1. To do so, I used the following syntax:

inlamod1a005=inla(formula=dxyz~type+f(pid,model="iid")+ f(tsv,model="rw1", scale.model = TRUE,hyper = list(theta = list(prior='pc.prec', param=c(X,0.01)))),data=inladat)

where by trial and error I used several values of X (0.05,1,2,2.5,2.65, 2.75,3,4,5). The results are surprising to me, as I actually can't control the smooth. The smooth behaviour is on-off pattern: it is either the same as I got without specifying the prior explicitly (see plot above, for values 0.05,1,2,2.5,2.65) or a horizontal line (see plot below, for values 2.75,3,4,5), so no varying degrees of smoothness. Can someone explain what might be going on and how one would effectively tune the degree of smoothness

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-JH9dbMnMmCs/WrjbWRCw5QI/AAAAAAAAYFI/TEKmmy7hrqQKLmYqYk3YrUe--7EGFKWZACLcBGAs/s1600/tsv2.JPG>

Many thanks

Tiago

If you want to control the smoothness "manually", I would do this by fixing the hyper-parameters to different values. They control the signal-to-noise ratios, resulting in different "smoothness look". More noise usually means smoother signal. More differentiability (rw2) means smoother signal. These two types of smoothness are completely different concepts.

See for example the shiny app you can download at
https://haakonbakka.bitbucket.io/btopic115.html
for fixing different hyperparameter values. (This webpage is only a draft version)

Regards,
Haakon

I think you can deal with the Gaussian variables: The beta_j are correlated when they come from one model. This correlation matrix can be used in the next step.
- Note that correlation in beta_j and in x_j are related but not the same thing.

I also think you can deal with correlation between hyper-parameters (using the joint posterior). I have not seen the feature Haavard mentioned, but I am assuming it does this.

What I think is very hard to deal with is dependency (including correlation) between the hyper-parameters and the beta_j. For simple GLM models this could maybe be solved by making all parameters into hyper-parameters. For complex models, one could consider fixing the hyper-parameters and not doing inference on them in the second step (the second dataset).

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the interesting discussion.  In my simple example model, the only hyperparameter is the precision of the observed values for the response variable.  If the model does a good job of explaining the data x, then I would expect the residuals to be distributed normally with respect to x.  If residual analysis showed heteroscedascicity, I would infer that my choice of model was not appropriate.  That's a dependence between the hyperparameter and the covariate, though, not beta_j, so ... is there some other kind of dependence you're thinking of?

I bet a minimal example that shows the danger would help.  What is the most simple data generating process and (appropriate) model that demonstrates the kind of problematic dependence that you have in mind, one between the fixed-effect estimates and the hyperparameter estimates?  I can't think of one, but I'm not done reading the Wang, Yue, and Faraway book yet.

I think that the only way the concern could be specific to Bayesian updating and not model building in general is if there's something important in the model that is missing from the inla result or unsupported as a prior.  I'd be really interested to find out if there's some limitation like that, but I haven't encountered one yet.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I've been comparing a few simple models run using inla and lm based packages and wondered if someone could help me understand the source of variation between model results I'm finding. While I find fairly consistent results for random effects models, there are some notable differences between models run in inla and lm using a categorical fixed effect for locations.

Specifically, I find that a model run on panel data where location is treated as a categorical variable run in inla

> FE<-y ~ 1 + x1 + x2 + factor(LocID)
> OUT<-inla(FE, family = "gaussian", data=mydf, verbose=TRUE, control.predictor=list(compute=FALSE), control.compute=list(dic=TRUE))

 returns the following

> Fixed effects:
> > >    mean      sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant     mode kld
> (Intercept)       160.9964  2.6684   155.7567 160.9966   166.2301 160.9972   0
> x1                 -0.0304  0.0011    -0.0326  -0.0304    -0.0282  -0.0304   0
>  x2                  0.0358  0.0012     0.0335   0.0358     0.0382   0.0358   0
> factor(LocID)2     13.8265  9.5081    -4.8425  13.8266    32.4777  13.8277   0
> factor(LocID)3     30.4883 10.1403    10.5779  30.4885    50.3794  30.4898   0
> factor(LocID)4      0.0000 31.6228   -62.0862  -0.0009    62.0343   0.0000   0

while the same model run in lm

> FE.lm<-lm(y~x1 + x2 + factor(LocID), data=mydf)
> summary(FE.lm)

returns

>  Coefficients:
> > >    Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
>  (Intercept)        2.280e+02  1.996e+01  11.423  < 2e-16 ***
>    x1                -6.033e-02  2.432e-03 -24.801  < 2e-16 ***
>    x2                 3.492e-02  1.430e-03  24.421  < 2e-16 ***
>    factor(LocID)2     4.730e+01  2.077e+01   2.278 0.022769 *
>   factor(LocID)3     6.048e+01  2.113e+01   2.862 0.004218 **
>    factor(LocID)5    -8.071e+00  2.166e+01  -0.373 0.709392

such that there is a significant difference in the estimate for x1.

In addition, I find that for a cross-section of this panel data inla returns the same results for models run without location effects, with locations as a categorical fixed effects, and for locations as a random effect. While the random effects model is consistent with a model run in lme, I would normally expect the model with the categorical fixed effect for location to return non-significant effects for x1 and x2, or at least indicate that there is no residual variation remaining (this dataset contains only one record per location index).

Any guidance on understanding the differences between these model results is appreciated!  Example data and script are attached.

Check that your input data has observations for all the levels, and reconstruct it differently if it doesn’t.

Finn
